notes: From "good" and "message." In the Greek world it was the announcement of a victory or of a ruler's accession; Isaiah 40 and 52 use the verb for the news of God's coming reign. Mark's first line, "the beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ," may serve as a title for the whole book, and Jesus' own first words are about believing it (1:15). English "gospel" comes from Old English "good news."

range.note: An announcement of something joyful.
News of a king's triumph or accession.
The message about Jesus, later also a name for books like Mark.

elsewhere.note: "I am not ashamed of the gospel."

notes: An adverb meaning "right away" or "straightaway," and the signature word of Mark's style. It's used dozens of times in the book, as a connector that keeps the story moving at speed: Jesus is baptized and "immediately" the Spirit drives him into the wilderness (1:10, 1:12). Sometimes it means exactly that, and sometimes it is more a storyteller's "then." The same Greek root also means "straight" (1:3).

range.note: Right away, with no delay.
A storyteller's connecting word.
As in "make his paths straight."

notes: Empty, uninhabited, wild: the open country away from towns. In Scripture the wilderness is where Israel was formed after the exodus and tested for forty years, and where prophets like Elijah met God. In Mark it's where John preaches (1:3-4), where Jesus is tested (1:12-13), and where he goes to pray and to be alone (1:35, 1:45, 6:31-32).

range.note: Empty of people.
Wild, open country.
Where someone goes to be alone.

elsewhere.note: John preaches in the wilderness of Judea.

notes: To rebuke or to order sharply. Mark uses it for what Jesus says to unclean spirits (1:25), the wind (4:39), and, with the same sternness, his own disciples when they begin to say who he is (8:30). It's also the word for what Peter does to Jesus in 8:32, and what Jesus does to Peter in 8:33.

range.note: Speak sharply against.
Give a strict order, often to silence.
Charge someone strongly.

elsewhere.note: He rebuked the winds and the sea.

The one robber rebuked the other.

notes: Not purified: ritually unclean, unfit to come near what is holy. In Mark it is the usual label for evil spirits ("unclean spirit"), which shows how Mark pictures them: forces that defile and cut a person off from God's people. People also become unclean through disease, death, and certain foods, and much of Mark's story crosses those boundaries.

range.note: Impure under the law.
As in "unclean spirit."
Defiled in a deeper sense.

notes: Someone who has missed the mark: a sinner. In the Gospels it often labels people thought to live outside faithful observance of the law, such as tax collectors, so "tax collectors and sinners" is a phrase for the outcast. Jesus' meals with them are among the clearest signs of what he came to do.

range.note: One who has sinned.
Someone seen as outside the faithful community.

elsewhere.note: Many tax collectors and sinners came and sat with him.
A woman who was a sinner anoints him.

notes: To speak abusively, and especially to speak against God or what is holy. Jesus is accused of it when he forgives sins (2:7) and again at his trial (14:64). When Jesus warns about blaspheming the Holy Spirit (3:29), the context is people who call the Spirit's work evil.
uncertain: Exactly what "blasphemy against the Holy Spirit" covers has been debated through church history; in Mark 3 it follows the charge that Jesus works by an unclean spirit.

range.note: Speak abusively of someone.
Speak against God.

elsewhere.note: The scribes: "This man blasphemes."

notes: To be afraid, and also to revere or stand in awe. Mark is full of fear: in the storm (4:41), among the Gerasenes (5:15), at the empty tomb (16:8, the last word of the book in the earliest manuscripts). The word can mean ordinary terror or the awe due to God, and Mark often lets both meanings sit together.

range.note: Feel terror or alarm.
Stand in awe, as before God.

elsewhere.note: "Don't be afraid of those who kill the body."
"Don't be afraid, Mary."

notes: Literally "to change one's mind," but in the Bible it means turning around: a change of heart and direction toward God. Behind it stands the Hebrew prophets' call to "turn" (shuv). It's the first word of John's preaching of a "baptism of repentance" (1:4, the related noun) and of Jesus' own first words in Mark (1:15).

notes: The Greek form of the Hebrew shabbat, the seventh day of rest from Friday evening to Saturday evening. Keeping it was one of the clearest marks of Jewish identity, and it's the setting of three early conflicts in Mark (2:23-3:6) and of Jesus' first healings in Capernaum (1:21).

range.note: The seventh day, set apart for rest.
As in "the first day of the week" (28:1).

notes: A Latin loan word. A Roman legion was a unit of several thousand soldiers (often about 5,000 to 6,000). The spirits use it to say there are many of them (5:9, 5:15). Mark's readers lived under Roman rule, so the name would have carried the sound of an occupying force.

notes: A word that covers rescue, healing, and salvation. In Mark 5 it is used of the woman ("your faith has made you well," 5:34) and of Jairus' hope that his daughter will "live" (5:23), and in 8:35 of saving one's life. English cannot show that one Greek word runs through all of these, so the nuance can be lost.
